title: Number system
concepts: Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3… (using the convention starting at 1). Whole numbers include 0. Integers include negative whole numbers, zero and positive whole numbers.
Rational numbers can be written as p/q, with integers p, q and q ≠ 0. Irrational numbers cannot: √2 and π are examples. √49 = 7 is rational.
A prime is a positive integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors. 1 is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime.
A factor divides a number exactly. Multiples are obtained by multiplying the number by integers. Coprime numbers have HCF 1; they need not themselves be prime.

Divisibility: 2 → even last digit; 3 or 9 → digit sum divisible by 3 or 9; 4 → last two digits; 8 → last three digits; 5 → ends in 0 or 5; 6 → divisible by 2 and 3; 11 → alternating digit-sum difference is 0 or a multiple of 11.
Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. For positive divisor d, 0 ≤ remainder < d. Consecutive integers include an even number, so n(n+1) is even.
examples: Why is 13 not a factor of 36?
36 = 13 × 2 + 10. The remainder is not zero. Positive alone does not mean positive factor.
Find x if 47x2 is divisible by 9.
Digit sum = 13 + x. For a digit x, the only possible multiple of 9 is 18. Therefore x = 5.
A number leaves remainder 3 on division by 5. What about twice it?
Write N = 5k + 3, where k is an integer quotient. 2N = 10k + 6 = 5(2k + 1) + 1. Doubling the leftover 3 gives 6: one more group of 5 and remainder 1. Example: 8 → 16; remainders 3 → 1.
tip: Use divisibility before long division. Pair factors systematically: 36 has 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
practice: N leaves remainder 4 on division by 6. Remainder of 2N?

title: HCF and LCM
te: గరిష్ఠ సామాన్య భాజకం, కనిష్ఠ సామాన్య గుణిజం
concepts: HCF is the greatest positive integer dividing all given numbers exactly. LCM is the smallest positive common multiple.
Prime factorisation: for HCF, choose common primes with the smaller exponents. For LCM, choose all occurring primes with the larger exponents.
For two positive integers only: HCF × LCM = product of the integers. Do not apply this directly to three numbers.
HCF often solves longest equal pieces or maximum identical groups. LCM often solves repeating events next coinciding. Check what quantity is requested.
examples: Find HCF and LCM of 24 and 36.
12 apples and 18 oranges: maximum identical packets using everything?
HCF(12,18) = 6 packets. Each contains 2 apples and 3 oranges.
48 m and 60 m ropes: longest equal pieces without waste?
HCF = 12 m per piece. Number of pieces = 48/12 + 60/12 = 9.
Bells ring every 4 and 6 minutes. Next coincidence?
tip: For two numbers, find HCF first, then LCM = (first ÷ HCF) × second. Dividing first keeps numbers smaller.

title: Fractions
te: సమాన భాగాలు, భిన్నాల పోలిక మరియు లెక్కలు
concepts: In 3/4, denominator 4 counts equal parts in a whole; numerator 3 counts parts taken. A denominator cannot be zero.
Equivalent fractions come from multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number. Simplify using their HCF.
With equal positive denominators, compare numerators. With equal positive numerators, the smaller positive denominator gives the larger fraction. With different positive denominators, cross-multiply.
For addition/subtraction, use a common denominator. Multiply numerators and denominators for multiplication. For division by a nonzero fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
Remaining fraction = 1 − spent fraction. A fraction of the remainder has a changed base.
examples: LCM denominator 6: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Do not add denominators.
Spend half, then one-third of what remains. Fraction left?
After first spending, 1/2 remains. Keep 2/3 of that: 1/2 × 2/3 = 1/3 of the original.
tip: Cancel common factors before multiplying. For 3/8 of 160, calculate 160 ÷ 8 × 3 = 60.
practice: Spend 1/4, then 1/3 of the remainder: fraction left?

title: Powers and roots
concepts: aⁿ represents repeated multiplication for positive integer n: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, not 2 × 3.
Square: 7² = 49. Principal square root: √49 = 7. But x² = 49 has two real solutions, x = 7 and −7.
Cube: 4³ = 64. Cube root: ∛64 = 4. Negative cube roots exist: ∛(−8) = −2.
Same-base multiplication adds exponents; division subtracts them (nonzero base). A power of a power multiplies exponents. For nonzero a, a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
Prime factors pair for square roots and group in threes for cube roots. Perfect-square prime exponents are even.
examples: Smallest positive integer multiplying 72 into a perfect square?
72 = 2³ × 3². Multiply by 2 to make both exponents even: 144 = 12².
tip: For a positive integer ending in 5, multiply the preceding digits as a number by its successor, then append 25: 115² → 11 × 12 = 132 → 13225. Learn squares 1–20 and cubes 1–10 first.

title: BODMAS and algebra
concepts: Order: brackets, then powers/roots, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right.
Division and multiplication have equal priority. Addition and subtraction have equal priority. BODMAS does not mean always divide before multiply.
Nested groups: work from the innermost outward. A fraction bar groups the entire numerator and denominator.
Defined symbols must follow the definition given in the question. For equations, perform the same valid operation on both sides.

title: Ratio and proportion
concepts: A:B = 2:3 means A = 2k and B = 3k for a common scale k. It does not mean the quantities must literally be 2 and 3.
Order matters. Convert quantities of the same kind to the same unit before taking a ratio.
When a total is given, add ratio parts. When a difference is given, subtract ratio parts. A’s fraction of total in 2:3 is 2/5, not 2/3.
A proportion is equality of ratios: a/b = c/d implies ad = bc, with nonzero denominators.
Direct proportion keeps a ratio constant. Inverse proportion keeps a product constant. Fixed-job worker problems assume constant equal productivity and comparable working hours.
To combine A:B and B:C, make the shared B equal before joining the ratios.
examples: Difference 2 parts = 24, so one part = 12. Numbers 60 and 36.
tip: Use the value of one part instead of a lengthy equation. For 4:7 with A = 28, one part = 7, so B = 49.

title: Percentages
te: ప్రతి వందలో పోలిక; అసలు మొత్తాన్ని గుర్తించండి
concepts: Percent means per hundred: 25% = 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25. Percentage = part/reference quantity × 100.
Percentage change = change/original × 100. Ask “percentage of what?” before every calculation.
Increase by r% → multiply by 1 + r/100. Decrease → multiply by 1 − r/100. Multiplication by a positive factor below 1 reduces a positive quantity.
Successive changes multiply factors. Reverse a change by dividing the final value by the factor.
Percentage points measure the difference between rates. Relative percentage change compares that difference with the original rate.
examples: First increase = 100/400 = 25%. Reverse decrease = 100/500 = 20%. Bases differ.
600/1.2 = ₹500. Do not subtract 20% of the final salary.
tip: Swap percentages: a% of b = b% of a. 16% of 25 = 25% of 16 = 4. Break 15% into 10% + 5%.

title: Mean, median and mode
te: సగటు, మధ్యగతం, బాహుళకం మరియు భారిత సగటు
concepts: Mean = sum/count. Total = mean × count. Find missing observations by subtracting the known sum from the required total.
Median: sort first. Odd count → middle observation. Even count → mean of the two middle observations.
Mode is the most frequent value. There can be multiple modes. Under the usual school convention, all distinct values give no mode.
Weighted mean = sum of (value × weight)/sum of weights. For group averages, the weights are group sizes.
Adding a person changes both sum and count. Replacing a person keeps count fixed. Extreme values can strongly affect the mean.
examples: Four numbers average 15; known values 10,12,18. Missing?
Five people average 20; replace age 18 with 28.
Sum increases by 10; mean increases by 10/5 = 2. New mean 22.
tip: Assumed mean: for 48,52,49,51,55 use 50. Deviations −2,+2,−1,+1,+5 sum to 5. Average = 50 + 5/5 = 51.

title: Profit, loss and discount
te: కొన్న ధర, లేబుల్ ధర, అమ్మిన ధర
concepts: Cost price (CP) is acquisition cost; marked price (MP) is the label price; selling price (SP) is actual sale price.
Profit = SP − CP; loss = CP − SP. Ordinary profit/loss percentage uses CP as base. Discount percentage uses MP.
SP = CP × (1 + profit%/100), or CP × (1 − loss%/100). Reverse by division.
Markup then discount: multiply the two factors. Include additional expenses in cost when specified.
Equal selling prices, one x% profit and one x% loss (0 < x < 100): overall loss = x²/100 percent. This shortcut requires equal SP, not equal CP.
examples: Profit ₹200 = 25% of CP. Discount ₹200 = 16⅔% of MP. Same rupee difference, different bases.
Two items sold ₹120 each, at 20% profit and 20% loss.
tip: 25% profit gives CP:SP = 4:5. Two discounts a%, b% combine to a + b − ab/100 percent. 20% then 10% = 28%.

title: Simple and compound interest
concepts: Principal P is original money. Interest is additional money. Amount A = principal + interest. Keep the rate’s period and time units consistent.
Simple interest (SI) = PRT/100, where R is annual percent and T is years. It always uses the original principal.
Annual compound amount after n whole years: A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ; CI = A − P. Interest is added to the balance for subsequent periods.
For a stated nominal annual rate compounded half-yearly, use R/2 per half-year and 2T periods; quarterly, R/4 and 4T periods.
For exactly two years, same rate, annual compounding: CI − SI = P(R/100)². Simple-interest doubling time = 100/R years for positive annual rate R.
examples: ₹10000 at stated 10% annual rate, compounded half-yearly, 1 year.
tip: At 10% annually, two-year compound growth is 21%; at 20%, it is 44%. Two-year CI percentage = 2R + R²/100. At 12% annual SI, each month earns 1% of principal.

title: Calculation shortcuts
concepts: Use shortcuts after understanding the concept. Some techniques are commonly taught as Vedic maths; others are ordinary mental-arithmetic identities.
×5 = ×10 ÷2; ×25 = ×100 ÷4; ×125 = ×1000 ÷8. Divide first when exact and easier.
Numbers ending in 5: (10a + 5)² = 100a(a+1) + 25. Multiply a by a+1 and append 25.
Near base 100: (100−a)(100−b) = 100(100−a−b) + ab. The right part occupies two digits; carry if ab ≥ 100.
Assumed mean reduces large sums to small deviations. Ratio parts and percentage multipliers reduce repeated calculations.
examples: Cross-subtract → 95. Deficit product 2×3 = 6; pad to 06. Answer 9506.
Deficits 12 and 13. Left 75; right 156. 7500 + 156 = 7656. Carry 1 to left, keep 56 right.
tip: Choose the shortest reliable method, not the most elaborate trick. Estimate first to catch misplaced zeros and decimal points.
